title: Psychological safety
blurb: Recall what psychological safety is, why agile depends on it, its inclusion and contributor types, and how PRINCE2 Agile builds and measures it.
question: A team member feels accepted and valued as part of the team and can be herself without fear of exclusion. Which type of psychological safety is this?

teach.body: Psychological safety is one of the three success factors of agile transformations. PRINCE2 Agile calls it essential for a productive and innovative agile environment: people need to feel safe to express themselves, take risks and challenge ideas without fear of judgment or negative consequences. In plain English: in a psychologically safe team you can say 'I think this is wrong', 'I made a mistake' or 'what if we tried this?' and nothing bad happens to you for saying it.

Agile organizations rely on rapid feedback, collaboration and continual learning. Each of those needs people to speak. Feedback is useless if users and team members hide bad news; collaboration fails if quieter voices hold back; learning stops if mistakes are concealed. So psychological safety is not a nice extra: without it, inspect-and-adapt has nothing honest to inspect.

PRINCE2 Agile describes types of psychological safety from an individual's point of view. Inclusion safety: I feel accepted and valued as part of the team and can be myself without fear of being excluded. Contributor safety: I am encouraged to share my ideas and skills openly, knowing my contributions are appreciated and respected. The wider model these come from, by Timothy Clark, also includes learner safety (safe to ask questions and make mistakes) and challenger safety (safe to question the status quo).

teach.caption: Inclusion and contributor safety are the types named in PRINCE2 Agile rationales.

teach.h: Where PRINCE2 Agile builds and measures it
teach.body: Psychological safety is one of the key metrics for agility, with agile maturity and agile sustainability; agile maturity assessments begin in starting up or initiating a project. The project kickoff workshop includes a psychological safety topic. At closure, the project closure workshop's lessons report covers psychological safety trends. Leaders build it day to day through servant leadership, respect for every voice and treating problems raised as learning, not blame.
teach.cite: PRINCE2 Agile V2 book 2.7.6, 12.4.1, Table 13.8, Table 13.19

items.label: First assessed as a key metric

teach.body: Wrenfield Hospice is building a volunteer scheduling app. In the kickoff workshop, team coach Hannah Okafor runs an anonymous psychological safety check: several people say they would not admit a mistake to the group. She sets a norm that problems raised are treated as learning, thanks people who raise them, and asks the most senior member to speak last in retrospectives. By iteration 3, a junior tester flags a data-protection risk early, which would previously have stayed hidden.

teach.text: Psychological safety does not mean avoiding disagreement to keep the peace. It means people feel safe to challenge ideas and take risks without fear of judgment. A 'nice' team where no one questions anything is not psychologically safe in the agile sense.

items: Psychological safety is a success factor of agile transformations and a key metric for agility.
Essential for a productive, innovative agile environment: safe to express yourself, take risks and challenge ideas.
Agile depends on it because rapid feedback, collaboration and learning all need people to speak up.
Inclusion safety: accepted, valued, can be yourself. Contributor safety: encouraged to share ideas and skills.
Built in the kickoff workshop topic, assessed with maturity assessments, reviewed in the lessons report at closure.

summary: You can now explain psychological safety as feeling safe to express yourself, take risks and challenge ideas without fear, and why agile's feedback, collaboration and learning depend on it. You can also distinguish inclusion safety from contributor safety and say where PRINCE2 Agile builds and measures it.

A.q: Which statement best describes psychological safety in PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Team members agree with each other to avoid conflict
People feel safe to take risks and challenge ideas
The project has a fully mitigated risk register
Team members are protected from changes to their roles
A.why: Psychological safety means people feel safe to express themselves, take risks and challenge ideas without fear of judgment or negative consequences (2.7.4).

whyNot.0: Avoiding conflict is not the aim; people should feel safe to challenge ideas.
whyNot.2: A risk register records project risks; it is not about how safe people feel to speak.
whyNot.3: Role protection is not what psychological safety describes.

A.q: A team member says, 'I feel accepted and valued here, and I can be myself without fear of being left out.' Which type of psychological safety is this?
A.why: Inclusion safety is feeling accepted and valued as part of the team, able to be yourself without fear of exclusion (2.7.4).

whyNot.0: Contributor safety is about being encouraged to share ideas and skills.
whyNot.1: Challenger safety is about feeling safe to question the status quo.
whyNot.3: Learner safety is about feeling safe to ask questions and make mistakes.

options: I am encouraged to share my ideas and skills, and they are respected
I feel accepted as part of the team and can be myself
I can rely on the team to finish my tasks if I am away on leave
I know the project board will approve the requests that I make
A.why: Contributor safety means being encouraged to share ideas and skills openly, knowing contributions are appreciated and respected (2.7.4).

whyNot.1: Being accepted and able to be yourself is inclusion safety.
whyNot.2: Covering for absent colleagues is teamwork, not contributor safety.
whyNot.3: Board approval is a governance matter, not psychological safety.

B.q: Which PRINCE2 Agile workshop includes psychological safety as one of its topics?
B.why: The project kickoff workshop includes a psychological safety topic, alongside team values and norms, the team skill matrix and dashboards (Table 13.8).

whyNot.0: The project canvas workshop covers vision, users, options, benefits, risks, scope, cost and value.
whyNot.1: The release planning workshop covers OKRs and updating the release map.
whyNot.2: The agile enablement workshop reviews Agilometer assessments and agile adoption risks.

B.q: Psychological safety is one of the key metrics for agility. Which are the other two?
B.why: The key metrics for agility are psychological safety, agile maturity and agile sustainability (2.7.6, 12.4.1).

whyNot.0: Velocity and lead time are delivery and flow measures.
whyNot.2: Collaboration and respect are characteristics of the agile mindset.
whyNot.3: Benefits and sustainability are performance targets, not key metrics for agility.

B.q: Which action by a team coach is most likely to build psychological safety?
options: Naming who caused each defect in the retrospective
Letting senior members speak first and sum up
Treating problems raised as learning, without blame
Recording mistakes in each person's appraisal
B.why: People need to feel safe to speak up and take risks without fear of judgment or negative consequences (2.7.4).

whyNot.0: Blaming individuals creates the fear that stops people raising problems.
whyNot.1: Senior voices going first tends to silence others and reduces contributor safety.
whyNot.3: Linking mistakes to appraisals adds negative consequences for speaking up.

C.q:
Which two statements about psychological safety are correct?
1. It is essential for a productive and innovative agile environment.
2. It means avoiding challenge so the team stays in harmony.
3. Inclusion safety means feeling accepted and valued as part of the team.
4. It is assessed for the first time at project closure.
C.why: It is essential for a productive, innovative agile environment (1), and inclusion safety is feeling accepted and valued (3) (2.7.4).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is wrong: people should feel safe to challenge ideas.
whyNot.2: Both are wrong: challenge is welcome, and assessment starts in starting up or initiating.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: maturity assessments, including this metric, start in starting up or initiating (12.4.1).

C.q: At Ridgeway Opticians, a junior analyst feels welcome in the team, but after her idea is dismissed in a workshop she stops offering suggestions. Which type of psychological safety is lacking, and why?
options: Inclusion safety, because she is not accepted
Contributor safety, because her input was not respected
Agile maturity, because she needs more training
Transparency, because the team's work is hidden from others
C.why: Contributor safety is being encouraged to share ideas and skills, knowing contributions are respected; dismissing her idea undermined it (2.7.4).

whyNot.0: The stem says she feels welcome, so inclusion safety is present.
whyNot.2: Agile maturity is a separate success factor; the problem is how her idea was treated.
whyNot.3: Transparency is a mindset characteristic about open information; the issue is safety to contribute.

C.q: Why does agile working depend on psychological safety, according to PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Boards need staff to accept decisions quickly
Teams must agree on every item before work starts
Rapid feedback and learning need people to speak up
Fixed time and cost leave no room for debate
C.why: Agile relies on rapid feedback, collaboration and continual learning, so people need to feel safe to express themselves and challenge ideas (2.7.4).

whyNot.0: Quick acceptance of decisions is not the reason; challenge is encouraged.
whyNot.1: Agreement on everything is not required; safety is about speaking up honestly.
whyNot.3: Fixed time and cost do not remove debate; safety lets people raise concerns.

reteach.title: The smoke alarm
reteach.question: Why does an agile team need people to feel safe to speak?

blocks.h: A smoke alarm nobody wants to set off
blocks.body: Imagine a building where setting off the smoke alarm gets you told off. People would smell smoke and say nothing. Psychological safety is making the alarm safe to press: anyone can raise a problem, admit a mistake or challenge an idea without being punished. Agile's short feedback loops only work if the alarms are pressed early.

blocks.h: What happens when a problem appears

blocks.text: Belonging (inclusion safety) and sharing ideas (contributor safety) are different. Check whether the stem is about being accepted or about input being respected.

explain.body: Feeling safe to express yourself, take risks and challenge ideas without fear of judgment or negative consequences; essential for a productive, innovative agile environment (2.7.4).

test.q: Without what do people in a psychologically safe team feel able to challenge ideas?
test.why: Psychological safety means challenging ideas without fear of judgment or negative consequences (2.7.4).

whyNot.1: Approval is a governance matter, not part of the definition.
whyNot.2: Agendas structure meetings; they are not part of the definition.
whyNot.3: A coach can help, but the definition is about the absence of fear.

explain.body: Inclusion safety: accepted, valued, can be yourself. Contributor safety: encouraged to share ideas and skills, contributions respected (2.7.4).

test.q: A developer is confident that the ideas and skills she shares will be appreciated and respected. Which type of psychological safety is this?
test.why: Sharing ideas and skills, knowing contributions are respected, is contributor safety (2.7.4).

whyNot.0: Inclusion safety is about being accepted and able to be yourself.
whyNot.1: Challenger safety is about questioning the status quo.
whyNot.2: Learner safety is about asking questions and making mistakes.

explain.body: Rapid feedback, collaboration and continual learning all depend on people speaking up without fear (2.7.4).

test.q: Which agile features does PRINCE2 Agile link to the need for psychological safety?
options: Detailed up-front plans and formal sign-off
test.why: Agile organizations rely on rapid feedback, collaboration and continual learning, which need psychological safety (2.7.4).

whyNot.0: Fixed scope and long phases describe linear delivery.
whyNot.2: Detailed plans and sign-off are plan-driven features.
whyNot.3: Separate specialist teams are not what agile relies on.

explain.body: A key metric for agility (assessed from starting up or initiating), a topic in the project kickoff workshop, and a trend in the closure lessons report (2.7.6, Table 13.8, Table 13.19).

test.q: In which process does the project kickoff workshop, with its psychological safety topic, take place?
test.why: The project kickoff workshop belongs to initiating a project (13.4.4.2, Table 13.8).

whyNot.0: Starting up holds the project canvas and starting up workshops.
whyNot.2: Controlling a stage holds the progress review workshop.
whyNot.3: Closing holds the project closure workshop.
